How we got these numbers

  1. Start from this fall. October 1, 2026 enrollment by school and grade, split into dual-language, Oakton's ACC and regular classes.
  2. Age everyone a year. This fall's K–4 become next year's grades 1–5; kindergarten stays this fall's size; 5th graders leave for middle school.
  3. Apply the district's moves. Its Oct 28, 2026 count of K–4 students changing school on the Oct 23 map, spread over grades like the sending school. Each move also carries its share of kindergarteners.
  4. Add the program moves. Dewey's dual-language strand (102) goes to Lincoln as one class per grade; STEP (23) goes to Orrington. About 110 program and transfer movers the district didn't place by area are spread over the closing schools' destinations (left out in the low case).
  5. Count classes. Regular students per grade over the contract class-size goals (23 in K–2, 25 in 3–5), rounded up, plus dual-language and ACC sections. The range also tries goals one higher. On this fall the rule predicts 145 classes vs. 139 actual.
  6. Compare with rooms and seats. Classrooms from the district's Oct 6 room sheet. Seats are the smaller of the district's capacity table and the 2022 Cordogan Clark study.

Impact analysis · middle schools · Oct 23, 2026 draft

Nichols' feeder area shrinks; Chute's grows

Each elementary school feeds one middle school: Chute (Dawes, Oakton, Walker), Nichols (Dewey, Lincoln, Washington), Haven (Foster, Lincolnwood, Orrington, Willard). King Arts runs K–8. When the draft moves a neighborhood to an elementary school in another feeder, its middle school changes too. Hatched areas on the map are those neighborhoods.

Where the middle school changes

Students living in each area, our estimate (this fall's enrollment placed by 2020 Census geography). Includes program and transfer students who keep their placement. District count: 144 current K–4 students change both elementary and middle school, including 31 to King Arts by program or transfer.

Feeder areas, today vs. Oct 23

K–5 students living in each middle school's feeder area: the pipeline into grade 6 over the next six years. Enrollment and seats are this fall's (Oct 1, 2026; seats = smaller of the district table and the 2022 Cordogan Clark study).

What it means

  • Nobody switches middle school mid-way. Current 6th and 7th graders stay at their middle school regardless of address; the change phases in over three years.
  • It starts with this year's 5th graders. They enter middle school next fall under the new lines, and each younger grade follows. Families in the hatched areas who expected Nichols would be assigned to Chute or Haven.
  • Nichols loses about a quarter of its pipeline. Its K–5 feeder base drops from 1,136 to 843. Chute's grows by about a fifth. Chute has room (588 enrolled, 792 seats); the district hasn't said what Nichols' smaller pipeline means for its staffing or programs.
  • Dual-language and STEP. Dewey's strand moves to Lincoln, which also feeds Nichols. STEP moves from Lincolnwood to Orrington, both Haven feeders.

Not yet answered

  • Do siblings of current Nichols students in the hatched areas get to follow them?
  • Busing for students allowed to stay at their current middle school outside the new area.
  • The district's projected enrollment by middle school under the Oct 23 lines.

Impact analysis · Oct 23, 2026 draft

Who this draft moves, how far, and what comes with it

Dewey and Lincolnwood close. Their families and some families at four open schools get a new school. Below: what that does to walks, crossings, programs and the schools that take them in. Each point has a button that sets the map to show it.

Pick a school

Six things this draft does

1Most families who change school walk farther

Students in reassigned areas go from an average 0.62 to 0.93 miles. The number walking over a mile quadruples, 78 to 312. About 11 pass 1½ miles, the state busing line. The biggest jumps come where a closing school's families split off to a farther building.

Walk = street distance from home block to school. Students are our estimate; the district's K–4 count is in grey.

2More children cross busy roads to get to school

Students whose route crosses a district hazard go from 56 to 140. Most of the new ones cross Dempster (about 58, Dewey → Washington) or McCormick (about 58, Lincolnwood → Foster); Green Bay adds 15. Counting busy streets that aren't on the hazard list, new routes cross Central (256), Dempster (247) and Oakton (167).

No crossing guards, signals or crosswalk work have been announced or priced for these routes.

3Program students take the longest moves

Placements follow the program, not the address. Dewey's dual-language strand (102 students) moves to Lincoln as a group, 1.47 miles and across Dempster. Lincolnwood's STEP program (23 students), which serves students with disabilities, moves to Orrington, 1.81 miles. After the move every dual-language strand except Foster's sits south of Dempster.

The district hasn't said what busing these students get.

4The receiving schools fill up, two to the edge

On our projection for next fall, Willard takes most of Lincolnwood and reaches about 96% of its seats. Willard and Oakton could run short of classrooms (Willard 20–25 classes for 23 rooms, Oakton 25–26 for 24). Washington, Lincoln and Dawes also grow. Willard has the worst building condition score of any elementary school assessed.

Charts, the school-by-school table and how we got these numbers open under the map.

5Planned growth lands on Lincoln

Dewey's area holds the largest share of children living near the CTA and Metra stations, where the city plans denser growth. On this draft that ground goes mainly to Lincoln. Seven of 11 tracked housing projects are there. Together they add an estimated 11–94 K–5 students once full, 8–82 of them in Lincoln's new area. At the high end Lincoln goes from about 81% to 95% of its seats, before any further building.

Most new homes downtown are studios and one-bedrooms, which house few elementary students. The family-sized affordable projects add more per home but are small.

6The heaviest burden falls on program students, not on any one neighborhood

We checked whether the longer walks land on neighborhoods with fewer cars, more limited-English households or more children with disabilities. Mostly not. Families whose walk grows by ¼ mile or more are, if anything, slightly less likely to have no car (8.9% of households vs. 12.3% elsewhere). Limited-English households are a bit more common there but rare in both (2.0% vs. 1.4%), and children's disability rates are lower there (1.7% vs. 3.0%).

The clearest burden is on two programs. STEP, which serves students with disabilities, moves 1.8 miles. Dewey's dual-language strand moves 1.5 miles, including 27 students in the Spanish-dominant group.

Some families come out ahead: about 134 students get a shorter walk, half of them on the Lincoln → Oakton move (0.93 → 0.49 mi), in areas where about 1 in 4 households has no car.

Neighborhood averages can't see individual families. On its Oct 13 draft the district counted 329 of 713 moving students as marginalized.

The closed buildings

The district keeps both. Dewey would be a swing school while other buildings are renovated; Lincolnwood would be held to renovate or rebuild. A November 2028 referendum is planned to build or fully renovate two schools. Reopening either building would take later decisions and money.

Not yet answered

  • Busing for the dual-language and STEP moves, and for students allowed to stay outside their new area. Is it in the $2.4M transportation line or the closure line?
  • Crossings. Which routes need guards, signals or crosswalks (Central near Willard, Dempster, McCormick, Oakton), and who pays?
  • Housing in the forecast. The 2024 McKibben study assumes about 120 new single-family homes a year and still projects decline. Reports don't say whether 605 Davis, 900 Clark, Custer or the family-sized affordable projects are included, or what students per home it uses.
  • City data. The development pipeline and comprehensive-plan growth areas aren't published as map data.

iHow the numbers were calculated
  • Students. This fall's K–5 enrollment (Oct 1, 2026: 3,484) placed where the 2020 Census found children ages 5–10, with each of today's attendance areas sized to the district's own count of students living there.
  • Who moves. Students living in blocks assigned to a different school on the Oct 23 draft than today. Program and transfer students are counted where they live, so this runs above the district's 660 (K–4 only).
  • Walking distance. Along streets, alleys and paths from each census block to its assigned school (U.S. Census 2023 road file; expressways and ramps left out), starting from the nearest side street.
  • Crossings. A route counts a crossing where its path crosses one of 18 busy streets or the Metra/UP and CTA tracks. Hazard segments are the district's 2026–27 list as mapped in the Legion of Data Nerds boundary tool (placed by hand).
  • Program moves. Walking distance between the two school buildings.
  • Students from new housing. Public K–5 students per home by bedroom count, from 2019–23 Census microdata for the Evanston–Skokie area. Low end: local rates in large rental buildings. High end: suburban Cook rates for lower-income renters. Townhomes use townhome rates. Unit mixes are published for 900 Clark, approximate for 605 Davis and assumed for the rest (each site says which).
  • Student density. Students per square mile, smoothed over about 0.1 mile. "With new housing" adds each site's high estimate around its address.
  • Lincoln's seats. Our Oct 23 projection (about 467 students, including Dewey's dual-language strand) against 576 seats, the smaller of the district's capacity table and the 2022 Cordogan Clark study.
  • TOD areas. The city's open-data layer of transit-oriented development parcels. The comprehensive plan's growth map isn't published as map data.
  • Who walks farther. Households without a car (table B25044) and limited-English households (C16002) by block group, and children with a disability (B18101) by tract, from the 2019–23 American Community Survey, weighted by students.

Sources: City of Evanston, Proposed Development Projects; City of Evanston open data, TOD area parcels; Evanston Now, How may city’s housing plans impact need for school closings?; Evanston RoundTable, Feb 10, 2025 (McKibben demographic study); U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2019–23 PUMS (Illinois); U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2019–23 tables B25044, C16002, B18101; District 65, Boundary Impacts for LODN (Oct 28, 2026); D65 Dashboard (enrollment by school, grade and TWI group; checked Nov 2, 2026: every school within 8 students of the Oct 1 counts used here, 5,413 vs. 5,415 districtwide).

      How the counts are made

      Students in 2026 (the starting count). The district reports how many students are in each grade (October 1, 2026: 3,484 in K–5 and 1,931 in grades 6–8 across every D65 school, King Arts included) but not where they live. This page places them where the 2020 Census found children of the same age. For K–5, each of today's 10 attendance areas is first sized to the district's own count of students living in that area (the "area counts" in its utilization planning table), so areas where more families use D65 schools, or where enrollment held up, keep more students: about 94 of every 100 2020 children in Foster's area, 78 in Dawes', 71 in Oakton's and Washington's, 64 in Dewey's, 56 in Lincoln's and Lincolnwood's, 54 in Willard's, and 51 in Orrington's and Walker's. Within an area, students follow the 2020 children block by block. Grades 6–8 are scaled evenly (64 of every 100) because middle-school attendance areas were not available. Area totals are firmer than any single block. Switch Count to "Children 2020" to see the Census children instead.

      Is the 2020 pattern still right? Families move, so we tested an alternative: age the 2020 Census forward to 2026 (children 0 to 4 in 2020 are this fall's grades 1 to 5) and adjust each census tract by how its children actually changed from the 2010 Census to the 2020 Census, which carries each neighborhood's net family moves (a method demographers call Hamilton-Perry). We had each version predict the district's count of students living in each attendance area. The 2020 pattern missed by 65 students per area on average; the aged version by 68; aging without the move adjustment by about 81. Moves matter, but the aged version was no better, so the map keeps the 2020 pattern. Neither fixes the largest misses, Foster (too low) and Walker (too high), which likely reflect where private-school families live. Sources: 2020 Census DHC and 2010 Census SF1, table P14, via data.census.gov.

      Children come from the 2020 Census (Demographic and Housing Characteristics file, table P14, single year of age), counted on every census block inside District 65. Blocks are small in Evanston, usually one side of a street, so the edge error is a few children per area. Children who live in Wilmette, Chicago or another Skokie school district are left out entirely.

      Elementary or middle. Elementary areas count ages 5 to 10 (K–5) around the 10 neighborhood elementary schools, and King Arts when it is turned on. Middle areas count ages 11 to 13 (grades 6–8) around Chute, Haven and Nichols, and King Arts when turned on, since it runs through 8th grade. King Arts' students and seats are split by grade: 274 K–5 students and about 401 seats in elementary view, 171 grade 6–8 students and about 250 seats in middle view.

      Straight line or walking. Circles measure straight-line distance. Walking areas measure distance along streets, alleys and paths from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2023 road file for Cook County, leaving out expressways and ramps, plus the short walk from each block to its nearest street. The canal, rail lines, the golf course and campus have few crossings, so walking areas bend around them. A walking area is drawn as the streets within that distance plus the lots that face them.

      How overlap is drawn. With "Every school nearby" or "Half to each," areas are translucent so overlaps blend their colors like a Venn diagram. With "The closer school," each circle keeps its round edge until it meets another circle; a home in two circles goes to the school whose circle it sits deepest inside: its distance divided by that school's radius. When circles are the same size, that is the closer school and the line is straight, halfway between the two. When you make one school's circle bigger, its line moves out and curves around the neighbor, so the neighbor keeps a smaller round area near its own building. Shrinking a school (by hand, or when it fills up) pulls its line back the same way. Choose "Always the closer school" to split every overlap at the halfway line instead. Walking areas are split the same way, block by block. With "Neither, show as shared," shared blocks are hatched gray. All areas are cut at the District 65 line.

      Overlap and gaps. A child can live in two or three areas. "Homes near two or more schools" decides where those children go: the closer school, every school nearby (counts add up to more than the district), half to each, or neither, shown as shared. Children outside every circle or walking area are unassigned: they count toward no school and no seats, and the table lists them on their own row.

      Removing schools. Any school can be taken off the map. Its children then count toward the remaining schools under the same rules, and expected seats and capacity flags update. King Arts starts on: it is the neighborhood school for a small area (roughly Dodge to the canal, Dempster to Church), though most of its students come from across the district. Turn it off to see the other schools alone.

      One school's radius. The main slider sets every school's radius; tap a school in the table and use − and + to change just that one. When a school fills up shrinks a school's area to the distance where the children inside it, times how many of every 100 children attend, would fill that share of its seats, so a full school's area stops growing. The stop follows the overlap setting: with "closer school," only the children a school actually gets count toward its seats. When a school stops, children just past its edge go to the next closest school whose area reaches them, and those still beyond every area become unassigned, so you can see who is left without a seat nearby.

      Capacity. Seats are each building's capacity: the smaller of the district's capacity table and the Cordogan Clark 2022 facility study (Dawes 432, Dewey 537, Foster 576, King Arts 651, Lincoln 576, Lincolnwood 432, Oakton 467, Orrington 432, Walker 432, Washington 530, Willard 533; Chute 792, Haven 936, Nichols 705). "Expected" multiplies the children counted for a school by how many of every 100 children attend, which starts at today's ratio of students at the neighborhood schools to resident children of that age and can be changed. Not every resident child attends D65 (private school, about 1 in 6) and the 2020 count is older than today's students, so treat expected seats as a planning estimate. A school is marked over capacity when today's students or expected students exceed its seats. Most of King Arts' students come from across the district, so its neighborhood count says little about its enrollment.

      Oct 23 proposed areas are the district's revised FY28 boundaries (Google My Maps layer "Oct. 23, 2026 Proposed Boundaries"), drawn dashed over the map. They close Dewey and Lincolnwood; use "Take Dewey and Lincolnwood off the map" to see where those children fall under the circle rules. The mover counts beside the table are the district's, not ours: students now in grades K–4 who change schools because of the new lines (Boundary Impacts for LODN, Oct 28, 2026).

      The district's seat target. The district says its boundary model pulls each building toward the middle of 75–90% of seats, with a penalty four times larger outside that range. The green band on each seat bar marks 75–90%, and "When a school is full" can stop circles at 82.5%, the middle of the band.

      Sizing schools and Even out. Each school's slider sets its own radius (or walking distance), up to 2 miles. "Even out" tries sizes step by step: it shrinks schools above 90% of seats, grows schools below 75%, and keeps the version with the fewest schools outside 75–90% and the fewest students left outside every area. It is a search, not a guarantee; when the schools on the map have far more seats than students, some will stay under 75%. Saved setups are shared with everyone who can open this page; a viewer who can't edit saves in their own browser.

      Child density spreads each block's children over the area around it (a smoothing distance of about 0.1 mile) and shows children per square mile.

      Limits. Both counts rest on where children lived in April 2020; the 2026 count moves the totals to today's students but cannot see new housing or families who moved within an attendance area since then (see the test above). About 1 in 6 children in D65 attend private school, and immersion, magnet and transfer students attend outside their neighborhood. School locations are their street addresses.

      Who attends. With the 2026 count, the rate starts at the share of D65 students at the schools on the map: 3,210 of 3,484 K–5 students attend the 10 neighborhood elementaries and 1,760 of 1,931 grade 6–8 students attend Chute, Haven and Nichols (about 92 and 91 of every 100); the other 274 and 171 attend King Arts. The 3,210 includes 683 two-way immersion students at Dawes, Dewey, Foster, Oakton and Washington, many of whom live in another school's area, so it counts students in neighborhood-school buildings, not students at their own neighborhood school. With the 2020 count, not every child goes to a D65 neighborhood school; some go to private school or a magnet. The rate starts at today's enrolled students divided by the 2020 children of the same age. It also folds in six years of falling enrollment since the 2020 count, and today's totals include immersion, STEP and transfer students who live elsewhere in the district.

      Matching the counts. Children and students are always compared at the same level: ages 5–10 (5,494 in D65) against the 10 neighborhood elementary schools (3,210 students on October 1, 2026), or ages 11–13 (3,036) against Chute, Haven and Nichols (1,760); both work out to about 58 of every 100. Enrollment is each school's total on the district's dashboard as pulled on October 1, 2026, and matches the sum of its grade counts. King Arts counts 274 students in K–5 and 171 in grades 6–8. The block-by-block Census total for ages 5–10 (5,494) is 26 children below an earlier district-wide Census figure (5,520) because of how blocks on the district line are assigned.

      Sources: District 65 enrollment by school and grade (dashboard pulled Oct 1, 2026) and attendance-area student counts (district utilization planning table), via the Legion of Nerds enrollment repository; U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census DHC, Illinois (table P14, census blocks), 2020 TIGER/Line census blocks and 2023 TIGER/Line roads and address ranges, Cook County; District 65 enrollment dashboard, Oct 1, 2026; District 65 2026–27 attendance areas and Oct 23, 2026 proposed areas (FY28 Proposed Boundaries map); District 65 Boundary Impacts for LODN sheet and boundary-model description, Oct 28, 2026; streets drawn from OpenStreetMap contributors.
